title: Varying Sentence Structure
keyIdea: Good writers reshape sentences for the reader. Combine short sentences with a joining word that shows the link: because or when makes one idea depend on another. Expand a sentence with an opener, a phrase or an appositive, and put a comma on both sides of extra information in the middle. Reduce wordy sentences by cutting words that repeat an idea. Mix long and short sentences: a short one after long ones adds punch.
familyTip: Pick a paragraph your child has written. Together, find two short sentences to join with because or when, one sentence to grow with a detail between commas, and one word to cut because it repeats an idea. Read both versions aloud and talk about which sounds better and why.

visual.caption: Combined, expanded or reduced? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: It rained. We stayed in. → Because it rained, we stayed in.
The cat slept. → The cat, a fat tabby, slept.
We returned back home. → We returned home.
She ran. She won. → She ran, and she won.
The bus stopped. → The bus stopped outside school.
The small little puppy → The small puppy

lab.caption: Flagship lab: combine two sentences two ways, expand a sentence in the right gaps, cut repeated words, fit an aim, spot slips.

kid: You can change a sentence in three ways. You can combine two sentences into one. You can expand a sentence with more detail. You can reduce a sentence by cutting extra words.
Combine with a joining word that shows the link. 'The storm hit, and the lights went out' just adds. 'When the storm hit, the lights went out' shows how the two ideas connect.
Expand with an opener, a phrase or extra facts about a noun. 'Suddenly, the dog, a scruffy terrier, barked at the gate.' Extra facts in the middle need a comma on each side.
Reduce by cutting words that say the same thing twice. 'We returned back home' becomes 'We returned home'. Then mix it up: a short sentence after long ones stands out.
adult: Ages 10 to 11, Years 5 and 6. The US standard CCSS L.5.3a asks pupils to expand, combine and reduce sentences for meaning and style. In England, Year 5 and 6 writers use relative clauses and commas to make meaning clear. Key words: combine, expand, reduce, conjunction, relative clause, appositive, fronted adverbial.

Joining with because, when or although shows how two ideas link. The word and cannot do that. To expand, add an opener that says when or how, a phrase that says where, or a few words that tell us more about a noun. To reduce, cut words that repeat an idea, such as back in returned back, or really in really very.

The most common mistake is thinking longer is always better. That leads to long chains of and. Be careful with commas too: extra facts in the middle of a sentence need a comma on both sides, and pupils often leave out the second one. When cutting, a common slip is removing a word that carries meaning.

In the lab your child joins two short sentences with and, so, when or because. They drag three add-ons into the right gaps of The dog barked, cut repeated words from two wordy sentences, choose the version that fits a writing aim, and check a robot's claims.

practice.prompt: Which version shows that the rain caused us to stay in?
choices: Because it rained, we stayed in.
It rained, and we stayed in.
practice.hint: Which joining word gives a reason?
practice.explain: because states the cause. and only adds, and two separate sentences leave the link unstated.

practice.hint: Extra information in the middle needs a comma at each end.
practice.explain: "my cousin" is an appositive that renames Max, so it needs a comma before and after it.

practice.prompt: "We returned back home at 6 pm in the evening." Which words repeat ideas?
practice.hint: Which words say what other words already say?
practice.explain: returned already means went back, and pm already means in the evening, so both can go: We returned home at 6 pm.

practice.prompt: A sentence has {a} words. You cut {b} words that repeat ideas. How many words are left?
practice.hint: Take the cut words away from the total.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} words. The meaning stays the same because only repeats were cut.

practice.prompt: A paragraph has {a} long sentences. You add {b} short sentences for punch. How many sentences now?
practice.hint: Add the new short sentences to the long ones.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} sentences, a mix of long and short.

pool.hint: Contrast means the second idea is surprising after the first.
pool.explain: although sets up a contrast: Although it was cold, we swam. and adds, and so gives a result.

pool.prompt: Where does the appositive go in "The dog barked"?
choices: Right after The dog, between commas
At the very end, after barked
pool.hint: An appositive renames the noun next to it.
pool.explain: The dog, a scruffy terrier, barked. The appositive sits beside the noun it renames, with a comma on each side.

pool.prompt: "The small little kitten slept." Which word can you cut?
pool.hint: Two words here mean nearly the same thing.
pool.explain: small and little mean the same, so cut one. kitten and slept carry meaning.

pool.prompt: After three long sentences, what adds the most punch?
choices: A sentence joined with and and and
pool.explain: A short sentence after long ones stands out and makes the reader pause.

pool.prompt: Which expands "The bus stopped." with a phrase saying where?
choices: The bus stopped outside the school.
The bus stopped, and it stopped.
pool.hint: Look for the words that tell you where it stopped.
pool.explain: "outside the school" is a phrase that adds where. The other two repeat or break the sentence.

pool.prompt: Which sentence with a relative clause is punctuated correctly?
choices: My aunt, who loves cycling, rode 50 miles.
My aunt, who loves cycling rode 50 miles.
My aunt who loves cycling, rode 50 miles.
pool.hint: A relative clause in the middle needs a comma at each end.
pool.explain: The clause "who loves cycling" is extra information in the middle, so it needs a comma before and after it.

pool.prompt: You join {a} pairs of short sentences, turning each pair into one sentence. How many sentences fewer is that?
pool.hint: Each pair of two sentences becomes one.
pool.explain: Each join turns 2 sentences into 1, so {a} joins make {a} fewer sentences.

pool.prompt: "Really very good" uses two words for one idea. A story has {a} such pairs. If you cut one word from each pair, how many words do you cut?
pool.hint: Cut one word from each pair, so one word per pair.
pool.explain: One word from each of {a} pairs is {a} words cut, and the meaning stays the same.

pool.prompt: Which version adds a detail without starting a new sentence?
choices: My aunt, a keen cyclist, rode 50 miles.
My aunt rode 50 miles. She is a keen cyclist.
My aunt rode 50 miles and she is a keen cyclist and she was tired.
pool.hint: Look for a detail tucked between commas.
pool.explain: The appositive "a keen cyclist" adds the detail inside one sentence without rambling.
